source_caption:
A carefree criminal roaming the streets of Paris becomes captivated by an ambitious American student, pursuing love and freedom while living as though each day could be his last. Their relationship unfolds through stolen moments, restless conversations, and constant uncertainty, gradually becoming a romance destined for heartbreak.

Defined by its effortless style, raw energy, and revolutionary filmmaking, Breathless transformed cinema with its unconventional editing and spontaneous spirit. More than six decades later, it remains one of the most influential films ever made, capturing the excitement, rebellion, and fleeting nature of youth.

Breathless (1960).

source_details.title: Breathless
source_details.synopsis: Breathless (French: À bout de souffle, lit. 'Out of Breath') is a 1960 French New Wave crime drama film written and directed by Jean-Luc Godard. It stars Jean-Paul Belmondo as a wandering criminal named Michel, and Jean Seberg as his American girlfriend Patricia. The film was Godard's first feature-length work and represented Belmondo's breakthrough as an actor. Breathless is an influential example of French New Wave (nouvelle vague) cinema. Along with François Truffaut's The 400 Blows and Alain Resnais's Hiroshima mon amour, both released a year earlier, it brought international attention to new styles of French filmmaking.
